transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-08-22
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Catalyst ML Platform Lead), Tom Reyes (Catalyst SRE), Janelle Ortiz (Catalyst CTO)
Shared: Redwood deck (slides.link/redwood-oom-deep-dive), benchmark spreadsheet (sheets.link/catalyst-bench)

[00:00:00] Ava: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we wanted to make this a hands-on deep dive into the persistent OOMs and the timeouts you saw in your cluster last week. i think we have about an hour, sound good?
[00:00:12] Priya: yeah that works, thanks ava. quick context — we're running mixed workloads, chat + embeddings, on a small fleet of p4d-like instances in a private VPC. we started seeing CUDA OOMs around 1k token sequences during some longer chat sessions.
[00:00:27] Tom: and to add, some of the errors were node-level preemptions as well, but mostly the workers report out-of-memory in the runtime and then the requests time out upstream.
[00:00:36] Liam: ok, that's helpful. a couple high-level hypothesis: 1) real model memory growth due to KV cache retention across long sessions, 2) batching spikes producing large aggregate memory, 3) quantization/kernel path regressions on the specific cuDNN driver you have, or 4) host pinned memory exhaustion (cudaHostAlloc) leading to failure to allocate.
[00:00:59] Janelle: would also like to know if this is only on the dedicated/persistent pool or also happening on burst/spot capacity; we saw different patterns there.
[00:01:10] Priya: primarily on our reserved capacity, but there were a couple on spot as well.

Summary / quick notes:
- Symptoms: intermittent CUDA OOMs, worker process exit, upstream request timeouts, occasional node preemptions.
- Frequency: daily spikes during 10am-12pm PST traffic.
- Affected models: 13B and 70B variants (fp16 and int8 quantized) used in chat workloads.

[00:02:00] Liam: first, let's walk through the runtime memory map. the Redwood runtime keeps a KV cache per session and tries to share weights read-only in GPU memory. when sessions grow long we keep large KV caches which are a major contributor. two important levers: a) KV cache eviction/pinning policy and b) batching/continuous batching window size.
[00:02:30] Priya: can you explain the eviction policy? we're currently using infinite session retention to support long conversations.
[00:02:36] Liam: sure — by default we keep the KV cache until session ends or until mem pressure triggers eviction. mem pressure is heuristically calculated, but it's possible that heuristics are too lax and we end up holding caches until the allocation fails, which produces a cudaErrorMemoryAllocation (OOM) at cuMemAlloc time.
[00:03:00] Ava: note — we've seen this before when customers pin the cache expecting perfect chat continuity. the tradeoff is latency vs memory safety.

[00:03:15] Tom: we do want continuity, but losing requests is worse. any recommended safe defaults?
[00:03:20] Liam: yes — reduce per-session max KV length, enable LRU-like eviction at 80% of usable GPU memory, and enable prefix caching for the most recent turns only. that reduces worst-case peak. also set a soft cap on batch size to avoid spike aggregations.

[00:03:50] Priya: second question about quantization — we run an int8 path for the 13B to save memory. could quantized kernels be causing misallocations? we saw some errors referencing cublasLt in the pod logs.
[00:04:04] Liam: quantized kernels can change memory patterns — sometimes extra workspace buffers or fallback to a different kernel increases transient allocation. cublasLt workspace is a common culprit. driver version mismatch can also cause larger workspace requirements. we should check your CUDA/cuBLAS/Driver stack.

[00:04:40] Janelle: the infra team pinned drivers last month to a 12.1 driver. is that known to have issues?
[00:04:46] Liam: driver 12.1 is generally fine, but specific micro-releases with certain cuBLAS/cudnn combinations can surface. we need the exact nvidia-smi, cuDNN, and libcudart versions from the failing hosts.

[00:05:15] Ava: can you also confirm if your worker containers use multi-process or single-process model shards? that changes alloc patterns.
[00:05:23] Priya: single process per GPU, multi-worker per node.
[00:05:27] Liam: single process per GPU is simpler; still, we need to check whether CUDA allocation failures come from cudaMalloc vs cudaHostAlloc vs cuMemMap. logs often show the call site.

[00:05:45] Priya: we copied one of the crash logs to the shared sheet (sheets.link/catalyst-bench). there's an entry with cublasLt error, then the process aborts.
[00:05:55] Liam: got it — we'll correlate timestamps. also check dmesg for OOM killer or kernel messages; sometimes host OOM leads to GPU allocation failures.

[00:06:20] Tom: there were also timeouts from our side — LB would see 504s because the worker didn't respond. is Redwood re-trying automatically? we saw multiple retries that resulted in duplicate expensive model runs.
[00:06:34] Ava: by default Redwood has retry semantics on certain transient failures. we have exponential backoff with jitter, but we also avoid silent double-exec by using idempotency tokens. if the failure is a hard OOM and the worker died, sometimes retries spin up new work but if the request body is large it can trigger the same condition.
[00:06:56] Liam: important to pick good retry rules: 1) detect worker process death vs transient network error, 2) implement a short-circuit for memory-failure errors (e.g., if we see cudaErrorMemoryAllocation, escalate to safe fallback model or reject with a specific 5xx that indicates size).

[00:07:25] Priya: that makes sense. is there a way to route problematic sessions to a lower-memory model automatically?
[00:07:32] Liam: yes — route by policy. you can configure a fallback to a smaller model or a quantized variant when runtime memory pressure is detected. Redwood supports automatic fallback routing with a policy threshold.

[00:07:50] Janelle: what about batching? we suspect the batcher occasionally aggregates many small requests causing a transient high memory spike. can you tune the batch window?
[00:07:58] Liam: absolutely — increase max batch size cap and reduce max batching time window, or enable per-customer batch limits. another approach is adaptive batching: the runtime will dynamically shrink batches when free memory falls below a threshold. we can enable that mode in Dedicated/private deployments.

[00:08:28] Tom: a couple of our ops folks also saw worker restarts tied to cgroups memory limits. could cgroup limits interact and cause container-level OOMs before the CUDA alloc shows?
[00:08:38] Liam: yes. if the container is memory-limited, host allocations (like pinned host memory, or staging buffers) can push cgroup over limit and get killed by OOM killer. we recommend sizing cgroups with headroom beyond GPU device memory usage.

Diagnostic plan discussed:
- Collect full logs: nvidia-smi, driver, dmesg, container/coredump, runtime debug logs.
- Reproduce with a controlled bench that mimics your traffic pattern (long-session + bursts).
- Run a kernel/workspace check on current driver stack.

[00:09:15] Priya: ok, we'll hand over logs. one more thing — on-prem constraints, we have restricted KMS and some HSM calls that can block startup and maybe cause timeouts; any pointers?
[00:09:27] Ava: for on-prem/VPC, any network/blocking call during model init can cause per-request slowdowns. ensure key unwrap isn't done synchronously on request path; Redwood supports pre-warmed key loading with KMS caching.

[00:09:45] Liam: and for private deployments, we provide an init probe that warms weights and pre-allocates common workspace to avoid first-request spikes.

[00:10:05] Tom: about retry semantics — can Redwood expose error codes to our LB so we can short-circuit retries for out-of-memory cases?
[00:10:13] Ava: yes — we can map runtime error classes to HTTP status codes and include a retry_hint header. we'll surface a 503 with Retry-After for transient network/timeouts and a 500-series with no-retry for deterministic OOMs if you prefer.

[00:10:40] Priya: do we have telemetry to show how often retry loops doubled work? that's eating tokens.
[00:10:46] Liam: Redwood Console traces token counts per attempt and can correlate idempotency tokens; we can generate a report showing duplicate executions per request id. we'll attach an example to the shared spreadsheet.

[00:11:05] Janelle: any immediate mitigations we can turn on?
[00:11:09] Liam: yes - short term: cap KV retention per session, enable LRU eviction, enable adaptive batching, set max_batch_size lower, and route large-session requests to the smaller model fallback. Also, turn on the memory-pressure early-evict flag. These are config toggles in Redwood Dedicated/private.

[00:11:40] Priya: can you walk through what we should include in the repro we send?
[00:11:44] Liam: include: exact request payloads (or sanitized), timestamps, model+variant, container id, GPU id, nvidia-smi output at failure time, dmesg, syslog, complete runtime debug logs (we can give a debug toggle), and also the driver's version output. a small script that replays traffic with the same concurrency and session lengths helps a lot.

[00:12:10] Ava: we'll also provide a sample repro harness and a recommended bench config that simulates long sessions with occasional bursts.

[00:12:22] Priya: we've also seen occasional hangs that look like cuda sync/timeouts, not memory — is that a different class?
[00:12:28] Liam: yes, cuda kernel hangs can occur with certain driver/kernel combos or if GPU hardware errors happen; those often show up as timeouts in the kernel (Xid errors). those require kernel logs and may need driver updates or avoiding a buggy kernel path.

[00:12:50] Tom: ok, so next steps — collect logs, run repro, and then deep debug on Redwood side. can we get an estimated timeline?
[00:12:58] Ava: we can run an initial analysis in 48-72 hours after we get logs and repro. if it's driver/stack related we'll coordinate with your infra to test patched drivers.

[00:13:10] Janelle: any notes about mitigate cost from retries? we're seeing double billing for duplicated runs.
[00:13:18] Liam: reduce retries, add server-side dedup via idempotency token, and short-circuit on known OOM errors to avoid re-exec. we can also add a retry budget per request to limit total attempts.

[00:13:40] Priya: great. can you send the security/VPC checklist now?
[00:13:44] Ava: yes I'll drop the link — security packet: security.link/redwood-vpc-packet

Recap (at end):
- Root causes hypothesized: KV cache growth, batching spikes, driver kernel workspace increases for quantized path, host/cgroup limits, and occasional kernel Xid hangs.
- Immediate mitigations: KV caps + LRU eviction, adaptive batching, lower max_batch_size, route to fallback model, enable pre-warm init probe, reduce retries and add idempotency enforcement.
- Diagnostics: collect nvidia-smi/cuDNN/driver versions, dmesg, runtime debug logs, and a replay script.

[00:14:20] Action items reviewed:
- Liam Chen: collect kernel/workspace checklist & repro harness, prepare sample bench config, and run initial local repro by 2025-08-25.
- Priya Nair: provide crash logs, sample payloads, and list of affected container IDs by 2025-08-24.
- Ava Martinez: share slides and benchmark spreadsheet links and the security/VPC checklist (DONE after call).
- Tom Reyes: open support ticket with infra details and attach node crashdumps.

[00:14:50] Janelle: thanks everyone, this was helpful. we'll prioritize the logs and aim to get the repro to you tomorrow.
[00:14:57] Ava: perfect, thanks all — we'll follow up with the analysis and schedule the deep-debug session next week.

End of transcript.
